label: prop:orbit
title: Theorem
head: environment
name: Invariant Bernoulli formula

label: lem:uniform
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:uniform}
If $\lambda$ is uniform on $\Omega$, then $B_\varepsilon(\lambda)=S(\Omega)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Every coupling satisfies $\langle A,\varepsilon\rangle\le\max_{a\in\Omega}\langle a,\varepsilon\rangle$, so $B_\varepsilon(\lambda)\le S(\Omega)$.

For the reverse inequality, choose a maximizing index $a(\varepsilon)\in\Omega$, breaking ties by a fixed ordering. Let $U$ be independent and uniform on $\Gamma$, and put
\[
 A=U a(\varepsilon),\qquad \varepsilon'=U\varepsilon.
\]
Conditional on $\varepsilon$, the point $A$ is uniform on $\Omega$, because the action is transitive. The vector $\varepsilon'$ has the same law as $\varepsilon$. Finally, coordinate permutations preserve the pairing, so
\[
 \langle A,\varepsilon'\rangle
 =\langle a(\varepsilon),\varepsilon\rangle
 =\max_{a\in\Omega}\langle a,\varepsilon\rangle.
\]
This is an admissible coupling attaining the desired value.
head: environment

label: lem:gibbs
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: Invariant entropy identity

label: eq:KL
title: Proof
body_md:
The row sums of \eqref{eq:gibbs} equal $\lambda(a)$ by the definition of $Z_\Omega(t)$ and its independence of $a$. Symmetry of $D_t$ gives the same column sums. Hence $Q_t\in\Pi(\lambda,\lambda)$.

For any $P\in\Pi(\lambda,\lambda)$, substitution of \eqref{eq:gibbs} yields the exact identity
\begin{equation}\label{eq:KL}
 \operatorname{KL}(P\Vert\lambda\otimes\lambda)+\mathbb E_P D_t
 =-\log Z_\Omega(t)+\operatorname{KL}(P\Vert Q_t).
\end{equation}
Relative entropy is nonnegative, and the last term vanishes at $P=Q_t$. This proves both assertions.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Combining \eqref{eq:external}, Lemma~\ref{lem:uniform}, and Lemma~\ref{lem:gibbs} gives \eqref{eq:orbit}.

Fix $a_0\in\Omega$ and put $Y_a=\langle a-a_0,\varepsilon\rangle$. Then $Y_{a_0}=0$ and
$\mathbb E\max_aY_a=S(\Omega)$. Since the joint law of $(Y_a)$ is symmetric,
\[
 S(\Omega)\le\mathbb E\max_a\lvert Y_a\rvert
 \le\mathbb E\max_aY_a+\mathbb E\max_a(-Y_a)=2S(\Omega).
\]
This proves \eqref{eq:anchor}.

For a Rademacher sum $R_a=\langle a,\varepsilon\rangle$, the elementary moment identities
\[
 \mathbb E R_a^2=\lVert a\rVert_2^2,\qquad
 \mathbb E R_a^4\le3\lVert a\rVert_2^4
\]
and H\"older's inequality give
\begin{equation}\label{eq:khintchine}
 3^{-1/2}\lVert a\rVert_2\le\mathbb E\lvert R_a\rvert\le\lVert a\rVert_2.
\end{equation}
Indeed, $\lVert R_a\rVert_2\le\lVert R_a\rVert_1^{1/3}\lVert R_a\rVert_4^{2/3}$. The triangle inequality and \eqref{eq:anchor} now give the upper bound in \eqref{eq:absolute}. The lower bound follows from
\[
 S_{\mathrm{abs}}(\Omega)\ge S(\Omega),\qquad
 S_{\mathrm{abs}}(\Omega)\ge\mathbb E\lvert \langle a_0,\varepsilon\rangle\rvert.
\]
The maximum of these two lower bounds controls half their sum.

title: Remark
body_md: After importing \eqref{eq:external}, the stationary application requires no further replication, Bernoulli decomposition, or construction of admissible partitions. This is a simplification of the application, not a claim that the external comparison itself is elementary.

name: Dyadic form

label: lem:laplace
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We first locate the height of $F$ at the threshold $\tau_n$ and then account for the large-scale tail.

\par\smallskip\noindent\textit{Threshold estimates.}\ 
If $t<\tau_n$, split the average defining $Z_\Omega(t)$ according to whether $D_t(a,b)\le2^n$. This gives
\[
 Z_\Omega(t)\le2^{-2^n}+e^{-2^n}\le2\,2^{-2^n},
 \qquad
 F(t)\ge(2^n-1)\log2\ge c2^n.
\]
If $t>\tau_n$, monotonicity of the balls gives
\[
 Z_\Omega(t)\ge2^{-2^n}e^{-2^n},
 \qquad F(t)\le(1+\log2)2^n.
\]
For each $t$, the geometric sum of $2^n$ over levels with $t<\tau_n$ is bounded by a constant times its largest term, and therefore by $CF(t)$. Integrating yields
\begin{equation}\label{eq:tau-lower}
 \sum_{n\ge1}2^n\tau_n\lesssim\int_0^\infty F(t)\,dt.
\end{equation}
Conversely, on $(\tau_{n+1},\tau_n)$ the upper estimate at level $n+1$ applies. The intervals with positive length partition $(0,\tau_1)$, up to endpoints, because the sequence is eventually zero. Hence
\[
 \int_0^{\tau_1}F(t)\,dt
 \lesssim\sum_{n\ge1}2^{n+1}(\tau_n-\tau_{n+1})
 \lesssim\sum_{n\ge1}2^n\tau_n.
\]
On $(\tau_1,\Delta)$, the level-one estimate bounds $F$ by a universal constant.

\par\smallskip\noindent\textit{The diameter term.}\ 
If $t\ge\Delta$, no clipping occurs, and $D_t(a,b)=\lVert a-b\rVert_2^2/t^2\le1$. The inequalities
$1-e^{-u}\ge(1-e^{-1})u$ for $0\le u\le1$ and $-\log\mathbb E e^{-U}\le\mathbb E U$ imply
\[
 F(t)\asymp\frac{\mathbb E_{b\in\Omega}\lVert a-b\rVert_2^2}{t^2}.
\]
The numerator is independent of $a$. Choose $u,v\in\Omega$ with $\lVert u-v\rVert_2=\Delta$ and average
$\lVert u-v\rVert_2^2\le2\lVert u-b\rVert_2^2+2\lVert b-v\rVert_2^2$. This gives
\[
 \frac{\Delta^2}{4}\le\mathbb E_{b\in\Omega}\lVert a-b\rVert_2^2\le\Delta^2.
\]
It follows that $\int_\Delta^\infty F(t)\,dt\asymp\Delta$. Combining this with the threshold bounds proves \eqref{eq:laplace}.

label: cor:overlap
title: Corollary
head: environment
name: Overlap formula

title: Proof
body_md:
Every nonzero coordinate difference between two indicator vectors has absolute value~$1$. Therefore
\[
 D_t(\mathbf 1_A,\mathbf 1_B)=\kappa(A,B)\chi(1/t),\qquad
 -\log Z_{\mathbf 1_{\mathcal A}}(t)=\mathcal L_A(\chi(1/t)).
\]
On $0<t\le1$, the last expression is $\mathcal L_A(1)$. On $t\ge1$, substitute $s=t^{-2}$ to obtain the displayed formula for $H_A=\mathcal H(\mathbf 1_{\mathcal A})$. Apply Theorem~\ref{prop:orbit}, noting that $\lVert \mathbf 1_A\rVert_2=\sqrt m$.
head: environment

label: lem:scalar
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The upper bounds in \eqref{eq:scalar} follow by retaining, respectively, $e^{-v}$ and $M^{-1}$ as lower bounds on the expression inside the logarithm. Also
\[
 q_M'(v)=\frac{(M-1)e^{-v}}{1+(M-1)e^{-v}}\ge\frac13
 \qquad(0\le v\le\log M).
\]
Integrate up to $\min\{v,\log M\}$ and use monotonicity thereafter. For \eqref{eq:scalar-integral}, if $L\ge a$ the integral is $a\int_0^\infty\chi(1/t)\,dt=2a$. If $L<a$, split at $t=\sqrt{a/L}\ge1$ to obtain $2\sqrt{aL}$.
head: environment

label: cor:separated
title: Corollary
head: environment
name: Uniformly separated set orbits

title: Proof
body_md:
For distinct sets, $2\delta m\le\kappa(B,C)\le2m$. Hence
\[
 M^{-1}+(1-M^{-1})e^{-2ms}
 \le e^{-\mathcal L_A(s)}
 \le M^{-1}+(1-M^{-1})e^{-2\delta ms}.
\]
Lemma~\ref{lem:scalar} gives $\mathcal L_A(s)\asymp_\delta\min\{ms,\log M\}$. After substitution of $s=\chi(1/t)$, \eqref{eq:scalar-integral} proves the signed estimate. The additional $\sqrt m$ in \eqref{eq:overlap} is absorbed: $m\ge1$ and $\log M\ge\log2$ imply
$\min\{m,\sqrt{m\log M}\}\ge c\sqrt m$.
head: environment

label: ex:singleton
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex:singleton}
Take $m=1$ and $M=\lvert I\rvert\ge2$. Then
\[
 \mathbb E\max_{i\in I}\lvert \varepsilon_i\rvert=1,\qquad
 \mathbb E\max_{i\in I}\varepsilon_i=1-2^{1-M}.
\]
In contrast, a purely quadratic cost would give an integral of order $\sqrt{\log M}$. The cap in $\chi$ records the saturation of a sign at size~$1$.

name: Why clipping is necessary

label: lem:integration
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $a=\sqrt{m/L}$. On $(a,\infty)$, integrate $m/t^2$ to get $m/a=\sqrt{mL}$. On $(0,a)$, write $t=au$. For $0<u\le1$,
\[
 \log(1+L/u^2)\le\log(1+L)+2\log(1/u).
\]
Since $\int_0^1\log(1/u)\,du=1$, the contribution is at most
$a[L+d\log(1+L)+2d]\le C_d aL$. This proves \eqref{eq:integration}.
head: environment

label: thm:interval
title: Theorem
head: environment
name: Cyclic moving windows

label: eq:interval-partition
title: Proof
body_md:
We first treat $m\le N/2$ by overlap geometry, and then pass to larger windows by complementation.

\par\smallskip\noindent\textit{The exact overlap profile.}\ 
For $A=\{0,\ldots,m-1\}\subset\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$,
\[
 \kappa(k)=\lvert A\mathbin\triangle(k+A)\rvert
 =2\min\{k,N-k,m\},\qquad 0\le k<N.
\]
Consequently
\begin{equation}\label{eq:interval-partition}
 e^{-\mathcal L_A(s)}=\frac1N\left[
 1+2\sum_{k=1}^{m-1}e^{-2ks}+(N-2m+1)e^{-2ms}\right].
\end{equation}
The coefficient of $e^{-2ms}$ counts the shifts with disjoint windows.

\par\smallskip\noindent\textit{The upper bound.}\ 
Since $\kappa(k)\le2m$, we have $e^{-\mathcal L_A(s)}\ge e^{-2ms}$. Also, for $s>0$,
\[
 \sum_{k=0}^{m-1}e^{-2ks}
 \ge\int_0^m e^{-2sx}\,dx
 =\frac{1-e^{-2ms}}{2s}
 \ge\frac{cm}{1+ms}.
\]
The same bound holds at $s=0$ by continuity. Retaining these terms in \eqref{eq:interval-partition} gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:interval-lower-Z}
 e^{-\mathcal L_A(s)}\ge\frac{cm}{N(1+ms)}.
\end{equation}
\Needspace{7\baselineskip}
Let $L=\log(eN/m)$. The two lower bounds on the partition function give
\begin{align*}
 \mathcal L_A(\chi(1/t))&\le2m\chi(1/t),\\*
 \mathcal L_A(\chi(1/t))&\le
 C\min\!\left\{\frac m{t^2},\,
 L+\log\!\left(1+\frac m{t^2}\right)\right\}.
\end{align*}
Integrating the first estimate gives $H_A\le4m$; integrating the second and applying Lemma~\ref{lem:integration} gives $H_A\lesssim\sqrt{mL}$. The baseline $\sqrt m$ is absorbed by $\min\{m,\sqrt{mL}\}$. Corollary~\ref{cor:overlap} therefore proves the upper bound in \eqref{eq:interval}.

\par\smallskip\noindent\textit{The lower bound.}\ 
The windows starting at $0,m,2m,\ldots,(M_0-1)m$, where $M_0=\lfloor N/m\rfloor\ge2$, are disjoint. Their sums are independent, so \eqref{eq:blocks} gives the required lower bound. Indeed,
$\log M_0\asymp\log(eN/m)$ for $N/m\ge2$. The signed independent-block estimate gives the same lower bound without absolute values. This proves both conclusions when $m\le N/2$.

\par\smallskip\noindent\textit{Large windows and the endpoint.}\ 
Let $m>N/2$ and $u=N-m$. Write $T_N=\sum_{x=0}^{N-1}\varepsilon_x$. Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:complement}
 W_{k,m}=T_N-W_{k+m,u},
\end{equation}
where the empty-window sum is defined to be zero. A single length-$m$ sum gives the absolute lower bound $c\sqrt m\ge c'\sqrt N$. The upper bound follows from \eqref{eq:complement}, $\mathbb E\lvert T_N\rvert\le\sqrt N$, and the already proved estimate for $u\le N/2$, because
\[
 u\log(eN/u)\le N\qquad(0<u\le N).
\]
Thus the absolute maximum is comparable to $\sqrt N$. For $m>N/2$, the right-hand side of \eqref{eq:interval} is also comparable to $\sqrt N$.

For the signed maximum, take the maximum in \eqref{eq:complement} and then expectations. Since $\mathbb E T_N=0$ and the vector of complementary-window sums is symmetric,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:signed-complement}
 \mathbb E\max_k W_{k,m}=\mathbb E\max_k W_{k,u}.
\end{equation}
No independence between $T_N$ and the complementary windows is used. This proves \eqref{eq:interval-signed}. At $m=N$, all windows equal $T_N$, so the signed expectation is zero.
head: environment

label: thm:boxes
title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For shifts satisfying $0\le k_j<m_j$, the overlap factorizes:
\[
 \lvert A\cap(k+A)\rvert=m\prod_{j=1}^d(1-k_j/m_j).
\]
The inequality $1-\prod_j(1-u_j)\le\sum_ju_j$ for $u_j\in[0,1]$ gives
$\kappa(k)\le2m\sum_j k_j/m_j$. Retaining only these shifts and comparing each geometric sum with an integral yields
\begin{align*}
 e^{-\mathcal L_A(s)}
 &\ge\prod_{j=1}^d\left[\frac1{N_j}
       \sum_{k=0}^{m_j-1}e^{-2msk/m_j}\right]\\
 &\ge\frac{c^d}{Q(1+ms)^d}.
\end{align*}
Also $e^{-\mathcal L_A(s)}\ge e^{-2ms}$. Hence $H_A\lesssim m$, while Lemma~\ref{lem:integration}, with $L=\log(eQ)$ and constants allowed to depend on $d$, gives $H_A\lesssim_d\sqrt{mL}$. The baseline $\sqrt m$ is absorbed as before.

A rectangular grid contains $M_0=\prod_j\lfloor N_j/m_j\rfloor$ disjoint translates. For $x\ge2$, $\sqrt x\le\lfloor x\rfloor\le x$, so
$\sqrt Q\le M_0\le Q$ and $\log M_0\asymp\log(eQ)$. Applying the signed and absolute independent-block estimates proves both lower bounds.
head: environment

label: thm:affine
title: Theorem
head: environment

label: eq:affine-count
title: Proof
body_md:
It remains to count the family. Counting ordered independent $k$-tuples in $\mathbb F_q^d$ and dividing by the number of ordered bases of a fixed $k$-dimensional space gives
\[
 \genfrac{[}{]}{0pt}{}{d}{k}_q
 =\prod_{j=0}^{k-1}\frac{q^{d-j}-1}{q^{k-j}-1}.
\]
Each linear space has $q^{d-k}$ distinct affine translates. Therefore
\begin{equation}\label{eq:affine-count}
 M=\lvert \mathcal A\rvert=q^{d-k}\genfrac{[}{]}{0pt}{}{d}{k}_q,
 \qquad
 q^{(k+1)(d-k)}\le M\le4q^{(k+1)(d-k)}.
\end{equation}
For completeness, after extracting $q^{k(d-k)}$, the remaining product has factors
$(1-q^{-(d-j)})/(1-q^{-(k-j)})$. Each is at least~$1$, and the whole product is at most
$\prod_{i=1}^\infty(1-2^{-i})^{-1}<4$. One elementary check of the last inequality is
\[
 \prod_{i=1}^\infty(1-2^{-i})
 \ge\frac{21}{64}\left(1-\sum_{i=4}^\infty2^{-i}\right)
 =\frac{147}{512}>\frac14.
\]
Taking logarithms in \eqref{eq:affine-count} gives
$\log M\asymp(k+1)(d-k)\log q$. Substitute this and $m=q^k$ into Corollary~\ref{cor:separated}.

label: cor:tails
title: Corollary
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The law of the coordinate vector is invariant under permutations, so Lemma~\ref{lem:uniform} applies unchanged. The Gibbs computation also applies to the cost $D_t^\Psi$. When the cost can be infinite, use $e^{-\infty}=0$ and restrict the entropy identity to finite-cost couplings; the diagonal ensures a positive normalizing constant and a feasible coupling. For indicator vectors,
\[
 D_t^\Psi(\mathbf 1_A,\mathbf 1_B)=\kappa(A,B)\Psi(1/t),
\]
with $0\cdot\infty=0$. The general-tail comparison therefore gives \eqref{eq:tails}. Symmetry and the same triangle-inequality argument as in Theorem~\ref{prop:orbit} give the absolute version, retaining the single-index expectation rather than replacing it without justification.
